Every router floods small notices about its own links (OSPF's LSAs, IS-IS's LSPs). Each then runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on the full map. BGP decides which exit to use; OSPF or IS-IS find the way to that exit. Big providers often prefer IS-IS: it runs directly on the link layer, not over IP, and copes well with very large single areas. Joining has two halves: registration (who you are, proven with the SIM's key) and a data session (an IP address and a path). In 4G the default bearer comes with the attach; in 5G the PDU session is a separate step.

In 4G: attach request → authentication (the network sends a challenge only your SIM can answer) → security mode → the MME asks the gateways for a session → attach accept with your IP → the default bearer is up. In 5G SA: registration request → authentication → security mode → registration accept; then the phone asks for a PDU session for a DNN (5G's name for the APN) → the SMF picks a UPF and an address → PDU session accept. Each step can be rejected with a cause code (for example "DNN not supported", "insufficient resources"). A modem log that ends after "PDU Session Establishment Request" with no accept or reject is a strong clue the problem is the session side, not the radio.
"Registered" on the router's screen only means the first half worked. Look for the session accept and an IP address before blaming anything else.

What is an APN (4G) or DNN (5G)?

The APN (4G) or DNN (5G) names the network you want: "internet", a company's private network, IMS for voice calls. The bearer (4G) or PDU session (5G) is the resulting pipe, with its own IP address and QoS.

One device can hold several at once: internet data, IMS for VoLTE calls (with a guaranteed-bit-rate bearer for the voice itself), a private APN for a company's routers. Each gets its own address and can go to a different gateway. QoS is set per flow: a QCI (4G) or 5QI (5G) number says the priority, delay budget and loss target - voice gets a better one than web browsing. A private APN with the wrong name or no subscription in the core is a classic "registered, no data" cause: the core rejects the session with a cause code that's only visible in the modem's log.
Typo in the APN on a router: registered, no data. The wrong IP type (IPv4 vs IPv6 vs both) can also be refused.

Non-standalone borrows the 4G core; standalone is 5G all the way.

NSA adds 5G radio to a 4G anchor cell: the phone signals over 4G and gets extra speed on 5G, but the core is still the 4G one. SA uses a 5G core and 5G for everything.

NSA (option 3x) gave early 5G its speed without a new core. Features that need the 5G core - network slicing, the lower-latency user plane, RedCap devices, the newer session handling - only come with SA. Latency on NSA is close to good 4G; on SA with a nearby UPF it can be lower.
A device that only supports SA in a place that only has NSA (or the reverse) falls back to 4G - working, slower.

Both start with a public colour, add their own secret colour and swap the mixes. Each adds its secret again - both get the same final colour; a listener can't unmix it.
